title: Uses of the Erotic: The Erotic as Power
description: An address delivered at the Fourth Berkshire Conference on the History of Women at Mount Holyoke on 25 August 1978, published first as a pamphlet and collected in Sister Outsider (1984): Lorde defines the erotic as a source of knowledge and power and distinguishes it from the pornographic.
plot_or_argument: Lorde begins by naming the erotic as a resource 'within each of us' that lies 'in a deeply female and spiritual plane' and that has been made suspect: women have been taught that the erotic is a sign of the inferior, the animal or the merely sexual, and the result is that the power attached to it has been surrendered. She distinguishes the erotic from the pornographic with the neat formula that pornography is 'sensation without feeling' while the erotic is 'feeling without sensation' - that is, the erotic is a mode of attention and knowledge that informs everything a woman does, from the making of a poem to the making of a bed. She illustrates with the difference between the demanding and the merely adequate in work, in friendship and in love; argues that the erotic is a measure of what we can ask of ourselves and others; and concludes that the erotic is a source of political power, because a woman who knows what satisfies her cannot be persuaded that she deserves less. The address is interrupted, in printed form, by its circumstances - it was delivered to an audience of historians of women - and its tone is the tone of the platform rather than the study. Its last movement turns from definition to obligation: to feel the erotic is to know what one can demand of oneself, and that knowledge is what makes political action possible.
narrative_structure: A spoken address in numbered sections, opening with a definition, moving through the distinction between the erotic and the pornographic, the account of what the erotic supplies to work and relationship, and the political conclusion; the paragraphs are short and declarative, and the argument advances by assertion and illustration rather than by citation.
meter_and_prosody: Direct address in the second person and the first person plural; short paragraphs with aphoristic closing sentences; a vocabulary that mixes the spiritual ('a deeply female and spiritual plane') with the political ('the erotic as power'); repetition and antithesis used as oral devices, as in the phrase that became its summary, 'pornography is sensation without feeling'.
historical_context: Delivered at the Fourth Berkshire Conference on the History of Women at Mount Holyoke College on 25 August 1978 and first published as a pamphlet by Out & Out Books; collected as the second essay in Sister Outsider: Essays and Speeches (Trumansburg, NY: Crossing Press, 1984). It belongs to the second wave's debates about sexuality and to the Black feminist critique of a feminism organised around white women's experience.
literary_significance: One of the founding documents of Black feminist thought and one of the most cited American essays of the period; it is a standard text in women's, gender and sexuality studies, it named the erotic as a political category, and it is the essay through which Lorde's thought is most often taught alongside 'The Master's Tools'.
bibliographical_notes: Delivered 25 August 1978; published as a pamphlet by Out & Out Books (1978) and later by Kore Press; collected in Sister Outsider: Essays and Speeches (1984) and in I Am Your Sister (2009). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The essay's central claim is that the erotic is a form of knowledge rather than a form of pleasure, and that the distinction between the erotic and the pornographic is the distinction between attention and consumption. From that follow its political claims: that women's distrust of their own satisfaction is a form of internalised oppression; that the energy of the erotic can be carried into work and politics; that the 'false belief that only the sexual is a proper source of power' keeps women divided from one another. The essay is also a link between the feminist and Black liberation arguments that Lorde made throughout Sister Outsider: the erotic is one of the resources with which difference can be lived rather than feared.
summary: A prose address in numbered sections in which Lorde argues that the erotic is a resource of deep knowledge and satisfaction that women have been taught to distrust, that it is not the same as the sexual and not the same as the pornographic, and that claiming it is a political act with consequences for work, friendship and love.
critical_context: Criticism reads the essay as a revaluation of a category that Western thought had placed below reason, as a contribution to the feminist ethics of pleasure, and as a text that complicates the period's debates between feminist anti-pornography and sex-radical positions; its relation to Audre Lorde's poetry of the same years, and to the tradition of Black women's writing about the body, has been widely discussed.
research_notes: The essay was read through the printed text in Sister Outsider as quoted in the sources consulted; the pamphlet's exact place and date of publication are given as the second-hand descriptions state them.

title: The Master's Tools Will Never Dismantle the Master's House
description: Comments delivered at the Second Sex Conference in New York on 29 September 1979 and printed in This Bridge Called My Back (1981) and in Sister Outsider (1984): an attack on a feminism that invites Black and lesbian women as tokens and a demand that difference be made the ground of political work.
plot_or_argument: Lorde speaks as a panellist at a conference marking thirty years of The Second Sex, and her remarks begin with the fact that the programme she has been invited to join has almost no Black women in it: the absence is the argument. She refuses the position of the token, describes the ways in which Black women and lesbians are asked to be present without being heard, and turns the conference's own subject - Beauvoir's account of woman as other - against it, pointing out that a feminism which makes the experience of white, middle-class, heterosexual women the measure of womanhood reproduces the structure it claims to oppose. Her central formulation is that the master's tools will never dismantle the master's house: the methods of a system cannot be used to end it. The address ends with a call to recognise difference - of race, sexuality, class and age - not as an obstacle to solidarity but as the material of it, and with the warning that a movement which cannot hear the difference within it will fail. The address is short - a few pages - and its force comes from the collision between the courtesy of the panel and the anger of the intervention: Lorde thanks the organisers and then tells them that their conference has reproduced the exclusions it denounces, and her own presence on the platform becomes the evidence for her argument.
narrative_structure: A short address in a handful of paragraphs, opening with the fact of exclusion, moving to the critique of the conference's theory, then to the general claim about tools and the house, and ending with a demand; the paragraphs are built as a sequence of assertions, and the last sentences are a warning and a promise.
meter_and_prosody: Direct, first-person, spoken prose with short declarative sentences and a few memorable formulations; anger held in formal syntax; the second person used to address the audience directly ('those of us who stand outside the circle of this society's definition of acceptable women'); no footnotes and no hedging.
historical_context: Delivered as comments at the 'Personal and the Political' panel of the Second Sex Conference at New York University on 29 September 1979, the conference marking the thirtieth anniversary of Beauvoir's The Second Sex; printed in This Bridge Called My Back: Writings by Radical Women of Color, ed. Cherrie Moraga and Gloria Anzaldua (1981), and in Sister Outsider (1984). It is one of the founding texts of intersectional feminism and of the Black feminist critique of the second wave.
literary_significance: One of the most quoted American essays of the twentieth century and a founding text of intersectionality; the sentence that gives it its title has become a proverb of political organising, the essay is a standard text in women's, gender and Black studies, and its argument about difference as the ground of solidarity shaped a generation of feminist theory.
bibliographical_notes: Delivered 29 September 1979; first printed in This Bridge Called My Back: Writings by Radical Women of Color, ed. Cherrie Moraga and Gloria Anzaldua (Watertown, MA: Persephone Press, 1981); collected in Sister Outsider: Essays and Speeches (1984). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The essay's argument is about the difference between inclusion and transformation: a conference, a movement or a theory that adds Black and lesbian women to an unchanged structure has not changed the structure. Lorde's terms are interlocking - race, class, sexuality and age are not separate oppressions to be ranked but a single complex reality - and her target is a white feminism that treats its own experience as universal. The essay is also a document of its occasion: the anger in it is directed at a particular room, and Lorde's insistence that anger is a source of information rather than a failure of civility became one of the most quoted arguments of Black feminist writing.
summary: A short address in which Lorde answers the organisers of a conference on Simone de Beauvoir, names the absence of Black and lesbian women from its programme, and argues that a movement cannot be liberated with the instruments of the system it opposes.
critical_context: Criticism reads the essay as the clearest statement of Lorde's theory of interlocking oppressions and as a key document in the history of the second wave's internal conflicts; its rhetoric, its use of the conference as a scene and its argument about anger have been widely analysed, and it is routinely taught with This Bridge Called My Back and with Kimberle Crenshaw's later work on intersectionality.
research_notes: The address was read through its printed text in the sources consulted; the date of delivery is given as the sources state it (29 September 1979), and the collection's own dating to 1979 in the anthology's list is consistent with it.

title: Against Interpretation
description: An essay published in the Evergreen Review in December 1964 and collected as the title essay of Against Interpretation (1966): Sontag argues that modern criticism has substituted the hunt for hidden meaning for the experience of art, and calls for an 'erotics' of art in place of a hermeneutics.
plot_or_argument: Sontag begins from a fact about the modern reader: that the first question asked of a work of art is what it means, and that interpretation - the translation of the visible into a hidden content - has become the dominant activity of criticism. She distinguishes two historical kinds of interpretation: the pre-modern kind, which sought to bring old texts up to date by allegory, and the modern kind, which she describes as 'excavating' and destroying, treating the work as a symptom of something the critic already knows (the Oedipal, the economic, the ideological). She argues that the modern style of interpretation has become a defensive response to the difficulty of modern art, a way of making it manageable; that it separates form from content, and that the separation is false; that the flight from interpretation is at the root of much of modern art's own difficulty; and that what is needed instead is a criticism that attends to the surface of works - to their descriptions, their textures, their ways of doing whatever they do. The essay's last sentences give the famous formula: 'In place of a hermeneutics we need an erotics of art.' The essay's method is to describe a habit of reading, give it a history, show what it costs, and propose a discipline in its place; its confidence comes from the assumption that criticism is a form of writing with its own pleasures, and its polemical edge from the conviction that most contemporary criticism had stopped looking at works of art altogether.
narrative_structure: An essay of some twenty pages in numbered sections, moving from description to history to polemic to prescription; the argument is carried by antithesis (form and content, depth and surface, hermeneutics and erotics) and ends with a compressed statement of aims rather than a conclusion.
meter_and_prosody: Aphoristic, confident, declarative prose with short paragraphs and frequent italicised terms; sentences built as definitions and reversals; a taste for lists and for the imperative; a first person plural that speaks for the age ('our culture', 'we are taught'), balanced by a critic's willingness to praise and blame particular works.
historical_context: First published in the Evergreen Review, vol. 8, no. 34 (December 1964), and collected as the opening essay of Against Interpretation and Other Essays (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1966), a finalist for the National Book Award; it belongs to Sontag's early New York period, when she was writing for the little magazines and the Partisan Review circle, and to the 1960s rethinking of criticism that produced the New Sensibility and the study of popular culture.
literary_significance: Among the most influential American essays of the century: it named a whole critical disposition, gave a generation its formula for describing works of art, and opened the way for the cultural studies and postcritique that followed; the essay is a standard text in courses on criticism and theory, and its closing phrase, 'an erotics of art', is one of the most quoted in modern criticism.
bibliographical_notes: First published in the Evergreen Review, vol. 8, no. 34 (December 1964); collected in Against Interpretation and Other Essays (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1966). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The essay's argument is about attention: to interpret a work in the modern manner is to replace it with a meaning that the critic already possessed, and so to lose the work's particularity. Sontag's alternative is descriptive rather than doctrinal - a criticism of form, of surface, of the sensuous life of works - and she connects it to the experience of contemporary art (abstract painting, the New Novel, the films of Bresson and Godard) in which the surface is not a veil over a meaning but the whole thing. The essay is also a document of the 1960s' argument with the New Criticism and with psychological and Marxist criticism, and of a moment when high and popular art began to be discussed in the same vocabulary.
summary: A prose essay in which Sontag describes the modern habit of interpretation, traces its history from the Greeks through Freud and Marx, argues that it has become a way of taming and diminishing art, and ends with a set of proposals for a criticism that would attend to the surface of works.
critical_context: Criticism has read the essay as the founding statement of a formalist and aestheticist criticism, as a transitional moment between the New Criticism and poststructuralism, and as a text whose influence on the 'postcritique' of the 2000s and 2010s has been acknowledged by its own originators; its relation to Robbe-Grillet's arguments for a 'poetics of presence', to camp and to the New Sensibility has all been discussed.
research_notes: The essay was read through the printed text and the sources consulted; quotations are short and confined to the sentences for which the essay is known.

title: Lost in the Funhouse
description: A story first printed in The Atlantic Monthly in November 1967 and collected as the title piece of Lost in the Funhouse (1968): a young boy's visit to a boardwalk funhouse at Ocean City, told by a narrator who keeps interrupting to discuss how the story is being told and how it might end.
plot_or_argument: The story is set in 1962 at Ocean City, Maryland, where Ambrose - the same boy who appears in the other Ambrose stories of the collection - has come with his family for the summer. He is thirteen, self-conscious, in love with his brother Peter's girl Magda, and he finds himself inside the funhouse, a maze of mirrors, a hall of illusions, a spiral staircase and a 'sliding board into the Atlantic'. Around this small adventure the narrator builds an essay: he discusses where a story should begin, how a personage should be introduced, what a plot is, why the reader's desire for an ending is itself a subject, and whether the story we are reading can have an end at all. Sections are numbered and interrupted; the narrator addresses the reader and himself ('you'); alternative versions of a sentence are offered and rejected. Ambrose gets lost, as the title says, and at the end he is on the sliding board or in the water, and the story has done what it said it could not do.
narrative_structure: Numbered sections, some of them lines long, which break off, restart and comment on themselves; the narrative of Ambrose's afternoon and the essay on narration alternate; the story ends with several possible endings offered and one of them performed, so that the reader cannot tell whether the story has closed or merely stopped.
meter_and_prosody: A deliberately literary, oral-sounding narrator with a taste for lists, rhetorical questions and essayistic commentary; parodies of nineteenth-century fictional address and of the conventions of the magazine story; long sentences that mimic the pace of a child's afternoon and short apophthegms about the art of fiction; typographic devices, including dotted lines and italics.
historical_context: Written in 1966-67 and printed in The Atlantic Monthly in November 1967, where it took third prize in the O. Henry Awards; collected as the title story of Lost in the Funhouse: Fiction for Print, Tape, Live Voice (New York: Doubleday, 1968). The collection followed Barth's essay 'The Literature of Exhaustion' (1967) and became, with the work of Barthelme and Coover, the standard instance of American metafiction.
literary_significance: One of the most anthologised American short stories of the postwar decades and the standard text through which metafiction is taught; the collection it names is a landmark of American postmodernism, and the story's devices passed into the common vocabulary of American fiction writing.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The Atlantic Monthly, November 1967; collected in Lost in the Funhouse: Fiction for Print, Tape, Live Voice (New York: Doubleday, 1968). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The story's subject is storytelling. Everything the narrator says about plot, beginning and ending is enacted in the story itself, and the boy's loss of himself in the funhouse is the image of the reader's and the writer's situation inside a fiction. Around that are the themes of adolescence - sexual shame, the discovery of being observed, the pain of not being chosen - and of the relation between life and the forms through which it is told. The funhouse is also a figure of art itself: a structure built to deceive the senses, which is exactly what a story is, and the story's narrator is aware that this makes him a maker of illusions rather than a witness.
summary: A story of twenty-odd numbered sections in which Ambrose, thirteen, goes to a seaside funhouse with his family and the girl he loves, and in which the narration constantly breaks off to consider beginnings, middles, endings and the impossibility of the task it has set itself.
critical_context: Criticism reads the story as a demonstration of Barth's theory of exhaustion, as a parody of the bildungsroman and of the reader's expectations, and as a story about the loss of the self that postmodern fiction is often accused of enacting; its use of the funhouse as an image of fiction, and its relation to the earlier Ambrose stories, are the recurring topics.
research_notes: The story was not read complete; the summary follows published descriptions of the story and the passages quoted in the sources consulted, and the record says so rather than implying a full reading.

title: The White Album
description: The long title essay of The White Album (Simon & Schuster, 1979), published complete in New West in 1979 from reporting done in 1968-69: a fragmentary account of Los Angeles at the end of the 1960s, opening with the sentence 'We tell ourselves stories in order to live'.
plot_or_argument: The essay opens with the sentence that has become Didion's signature - 'We tell ourselves stories in order to live' - and immediately complicates it: the stories we tell are 'the imposition of a narrative line upon disparate images', and when that line fails, the images are all that is left. What follows is a sequence of such images, most of them drawn from the Los Angeles of 1968-69: the empty house on Franklin Avenue with its 'particular vanity' of black-and-white tiles; the recording studio where the Doors are at work; meetings with the Black Panthers; a prison interview with Linda Kasabian, who is testifying against Charles Manson, and the trial itself; a visit from a man with a gun. Between these scenes Didion places her own case history: the nausea, the spells of vertigo she began to have in the summer of 1968, the psychiatrist's report, the outpatient clinic in Santa Monica, the chemotherapy she was told she might need. The essay's movement is associational; it quotes song lyrics, newspaper clippings, police reports, the psychiatrist's report, and its refrain is the impossibility of the narrative it is nevertheless performing. It ends in a hospital, with Didion looking out at the city and acknowledging that the story she has told is one of many that could have been told.
narrative_structure: An essay in a series of untitled fragments, varying from a paragraph to several pages, with reportage, quotation, personal history and reflection interleaved; there is no argumentative progression and no resolution, and the essay's unity is tonal and thematic rather than narrative.
meter_and_prosody: Short declarative sentences with a falling rhythm; the present tense used for scenes and the past for reflection; documents and testimony quoted at length and without comment; a repeated first person that is reserved to the point of impersonality; the phrase set in italics or repeated as a refrain.
historical_context: The complete essay was published in New West in 1979, from reporting done in 1968-69, and became the first and title essay of The White Album (New York: Simon & Schuster, 1979); portions of the material had appeared earlier in magazines, and the Los Angeles of the essay is the city of the Manson trial, the Black Panthers, the Doors and the aftermath of the 1965 Watts rebellion.
literary_significance: One of the most influential American essays of the second half of the century and a standard text in courses on the essay, on New Journalism and on California; Publishers Weekly named it one of the ten most important essays since 1950, and its first sentence is among the most quoted in modern American prose.
bibliographical_notes: First published complete in New West, 1979, from material reported in 1968-69; collected as the first essay of The White Album (New York: Simon & Schuster, 1979) and reprinted in We Tell Ourselves Stories in Order to Live (2006). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The essay's central subject is the relation between narrative and survival: people tell themselves stories in order to live, and the failure of narrative is a kind of breakdown. Didion's own illness is presented as exactly that failure, so that the essay's form - fragments, quotations, abrupt transitions - enacts the condition it describes. Around this are its subjects of California and the 1960s: the Manson murders and the end of the dream of the decade, media and image-making, the Black Panthers and the politics of the period, and the culture's habit of replacing events with stories about them.
summary: An essay in numbered fragments, moving between reportage - a Doors recording session, Black Panther meetings, a prison interview with Linda Kasabian, a murder trial, a psychiatric examination - and the narrator's own account of a breakdown she experienced in the summer of 1968.
critical_context: Criticism reads the essay as a formal breakthrough in American non-fiction - the subject as fragmentation, the writer as a camera rather than a narrator - and as a document of the end of the 1960s; its treatment of illness, of the Manson trial and of media culture has been widely discussed, and it is often set beside the New Journalism of Tom Wolfe and Hunter S. Thompson as a distinctively female and self-effacing alternative.
research_notes: The essay was not read complete; the summary follows published descriptions and the passages quoted in the sources consulted, and the record says so.

title: Sonny's Blues
description: A story published in Partisan Review in the summer of 1957 and collected in Going to Meet the Man (1965): a Harlem schoolteacher discovers that his younger brother, a jazz pianist and a heroin addict, has been arrested, and the two brothers slowly find their way back to one another.
plot_or_argument: The story opens with the narrator, a teacher of algebra in a Harlem high school, reading in the subway that his younger brother Sonny has been arrested for possession of heroin. He remembers their childhood - the father's bitterness and early death, the mother's request that he look after Sonny, the boy's early obsession with the piano, his truancy and his wish to join the army - and then meets Sonny's friend, who warns him that the addiction will not end with the prison sentence. For a long time the brothers do not speak. The narrator's small daughter Grace dies of polio while he is away, and he writes to Sonny in prison; when Sonny is released the two meet in New York in an awkward, careful reunion, and Sonny explains what music means to him - that heroin was a way of feeling in control, and that playing is a way of making the suffering bearable. In the story's final movement the narrator goes to a jazz club in Greenwich Village where Sonny is playing with a group led by Creole; the music begins as something the narrator cannot follow and becomes, in the last pages, a blues in which the whole history of the family and of the people is audible, and the narrator sends a drink to his brother and understands at last what he has been listening to.
narrative_structure: A first-person narrative in two large movements divided by a period of silence and a letter, with a long embedded recollection of childhood and a closing scene in the club; the story moves from the news of the arrest to the performance, and the two are joined thematically rather than chronologically.
meter_and_prosody: A measured, cadenced prose in the narrator's voice, with long sentences that reproduce the rhythms of thinking; dialogue in the idiom of Harlem and of musicians; the language of music used with technical precision; a final passage of great rhetorical power that describes a performance without quoting it.
historical_context: Published in Partisan Review, vol. 24, no. 3, in the summer of 1957, when Baldwin was already known for Go Tell It on the Mountain and Notes of a Native Son; collected in Going to Meet the Man (Dial Press, 1965). It belongs to the great period of American jazz writing and to the literature of Harlem at the beginning of the civil rights movement, and it is Baldwin's most widely anthologised short story.
literary_significance: One of the finest American short stories of the century and Baldwin's most widely taught fiction; it is a standard anthology text and a set text in courses on the American short story, on African American literature and on the literature of music, and its last pages are among the most discussed in American fiction.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Partisan Review, vol. 24, no. 3 (Summer 1957); collected in Going to Meet the Man (New York: Dial Press, 1965) and in Early Novels and Stories (Library of America, 1998). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The story's argument is that suffering can be borne and partly redeemed by being made into music, and that the blues are the form in which a particular American history has been carried. It is also a story about brothers: the narrator's respectability and his fear are set against Sonny's risk, and the story refuses to choose between them, since the respectable brother is the one who needs to learn to listen. Race is present everywhere - in the housing projects, in the police, in the fear of the dark - but Baldwin never makes the story a tract; the political argument is carried by the music and by the family, and the story's famous last image connects the singer's cup of trembling to the brother's drink.
summary: A first-person story in two movements, from the narrator's reading of the news in the subway and his memories of their childhood, through the death of his small daughter and his letter to Sonny in prison, to the night in a Greenwich Village jazz club when he finally hears his brother play.
critical_context: Criticism reads the story as a study in the ethics of listening, as a blues narrative whose form imitates the music it describes, and as Baldwin's most successful attempt to hold the private and the political in a single story; the figure of Creole, the function of Grace's death and the relation of the story to Baldwin's own Harlem childhood have all been discussed at length.
research_notes: The story was not read complete; the summary follows published descriptions and the passages quoted in the sources consulted, and the record says so.

title: Going to Meet the Man
description: A story published in Status in October 1965 and collected as the title story of Going to Meet the Man (1965): a white Southern deputy sheriff, impotent in bed, remembers his father taking him to a lynching when he was eight years old and finds himself excited by the memory.
plot_or_argument: Jesse, a deputy sheriff in a small Southern town, lies in bed with his wife Grace and cannot make love to her; his mind wanders to the black women he has known and to the day's work, when he and another officer arrested a young civil rights worker and Jesse beat him in his cell with a hose and a cattle prod. The prisoner, half conscious, asks him if he remembers 'Old Julia', and Jesse realizes that the young man is the grandson of a woman he once cheated in his mail-order business, and that he had known him as a boy. The beating resumes, and Jesse feels himself sexually aroused by it. The story then moves back to his childhood: the family car, a black neighbourhood singing 'Wade in the Water', his father's reassurances, and then the morning when the white people of the town gather to watch a black man burned and mutilated, with Jesse on his father's shoulders. In the last pages he comes back to the bedroom and finds that the memory has given him an erection, and the story ends with him turning to his wife.
narrative_structure: A single continuous present-tense night interrupted by two flashbacks, one recent and one from childhood, with the second flashback occupying the centre of the story; the return to the bedroom in the last paragraph completes the frame and delivers the story's judgement without comment.
meter_and_prosody: A third-person narrative confined to Jesse's consciousness, in a flat demotic Southern idiom; the childhood memory is rendered with the sensory immediacy of a child's perception and without explanation; the violence is described in exact physical detail, and the story's refusal of authorial comment is itself the moral instrument.
historical_context: Published in the magazine Status in October 1965, one month before the collection, and collected as the title story of Going to Meet the Man (Dial Press, 1965), Baldwin's only collection of short stories; it appeared at the height of the civil rights movement, two years after The Fire Next Time and a year after the murders of Chaney, Goodman and Schwerner, and it is one of the few works by a major Black writer of the period to enter the mind of a white racist.
literary_significance: One of the most discussed American short stories of the 1960s and the story through which Baldwin's treatment of white consciousness is usually taught; it is a standard anthology text on the literature of lynching and of American racism, and its narrative technique - full sympathetic access to a perpetrator - is regularly analysed in courses on point of view and on the ethics of representation.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Status, October 1965; collected in Going to Meet the Man (New York: Dial Press, 1965). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The story is Baldwin's most direct treatment of the sexual logic of American racism: Jesse's impotence and his excitement are produced by the same system, and the lynching is presented as the scene in which white masculinity is formed. Its method is to stay inside Jesse's consciousness, so that the reader experiences the banality of his racism - his self-justification, his nostalgia, his ordinary marital tenderness - before the atrocity, and then understands that the atrocity is not an exception to his life but its foundation. The title's 'going to meet the man' is both the boy's initiation and the sexual act the memory enables.
summary: A story that moves between a white sheriff's bedroom in the present and two memories - an assault on a young civil rights worker in his cell that day, and the lynching he was taken to watch as a child - and ends with the violence and the sexual excitement joined together.
critical_context: Criticism reads the story as an anatomy of the psychosexual structure of white supremacy, and debates the risks of Baldwin's decision to occupy Jesse's point of view; its relation to the Gothic tradition of the South, to the literature of lynching and to Baldwin's essays of the same years is the usual frame, and the final paragraph is one of the most discussed endings in American fiction.
research_notes: The story was not read complete; the summary follows published descriptions of the plot and the passages quoted in the sources consulted.

title: Letter to My Nephew
description: An open letter published in The Progressive in December 1962, on the hundredth anniversary of the Emancipation Proclamation, and collected as 'My Dungeon Shook' at the head of The Fire Next Time (1963): Baldwin writes to his fourteen-year-old nephew about what America has done to him and what he must refuse.
plot_or_argument: The letter is addressed to Baldwin's nephew and namesake, James, on the hundredth anniversary of the Emancipation Proclamation, and it begins by acknowledging that the occasion offers no comfort: 'you were born into a society which spelled out with brutal clarity, and in as many ways as possible, that you were a worthless human being'. Baldwin tells his nephew what the country has done to his father and his grandfather, and what it is doing to him, and then makes the turn that the letter exists for: he must not believe it, and he must not hate, because the hatred would be a second submission to the same lie. He explains that the white American is also trapped, in a dream of innocence that requires the Black American to carry the burden of the history he refuses to know, and he asks his nephew to accept his own humanity and his own history without accepting the definitions offered to him. The letter ends with an exhortation to love and to persist, and with the famous sentence about the country's future being in the hands of those who can say 'we'. Its argument is conducted almost entirely through the second person: the uncle's authority comes from his love, and the letter's diagnosis of white innocence is delivered not as theory but as something the boy will need to know in order to live, which is why the letter reads as both a private gift and a public document.
narrative_structure: A single letter of a few pages, with no sections; it moves from the occasion and the diagnosis, through the history of the family, to the reversal in which the nephew is told what he must do, and ends with an exhortation; the second person is maintained throughout, so that the argument is always addressed to someone.
meter_and_prosody: Direct address in the second person, with the cadences of the pulpit - repetition, antithesis, long periodic sentences that resolve into short declaratives; the diction moves between the colloquial and the prophetic, and the letter's most famous sentences are short and absolute.
historical_context: Published in The Progressive in December 1962 and collected, slightly revised and retitled 'My Dungeon Shook: Letter to My Nephew on the One Hundredth Anniversary of the Emancipation', as the first of the two essays in The Fire Next Time (New York: Dial Press, 1963), which became a bestseller and one of the defining books of the civil rights movement; the letter was written at the height of the movement, after the Birmingham campaign and before the March on Washington.
literary_significance: One of the most quoted American essays of the century and the standard introduction to Baldwin's political thought; it is a set text in American literature, history and civics courses, the essay through which The Fire Next Time is usually taught, and the source of the phrases about innocence and about the 'we' that recur in American public argument.
bibliographical_notes: First published as 'A Letter to My Nephew' in The Progressive, December 1962; collected as 'My Dungeon Shook: Letter to My Nephew on the One Hundredth Anniversary of the Emancipation' in The Fire Next Time (New York: Dial Press, 1963) and in Collected Essays (Library of America, 1998). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The letter's central argument is that American racism damages white Americans as well as Black ones, because it requires them to believe in an innocence that their history contradicts; the famous formulation is that the white man's 'innocence' is his crime. Against that, Baldwin sets the nephew's task: to know his own history, to refuse both self-hatred and hatred of the other, and to insist on a humanity that is not granted by the country. The letter is also a family document - the tone of an uncle speaking to a beloved nephew - and its intimacy is what makes its politics persuasive: the general argument is made through a particular relationship, and the 'you' of the letter is at once one boy and a generation.
summary: A short letter in the second person, in which Baldwin addresses his nephew James by name on the centenary of emancipation, tells him that the country has set limits on his life before he was born, refuses both the hatred and the false innocence that the situation offers, and ends by asking him to accept his own history without accepting the definitions imposed on it.
critical_context: Criticism reads the letter as a founding document of the literature of the civil rights movement and as a masterpiece of the epistolary essay; its argument about white innocence has been enormously influential in American studies, and its relation to the longer essay that follows it in The Fire Next Time, and to Baldwin's later writing on the same themes, is the standard critical frame.
research_notes: The letter was read through the text reprinted by The Progressive and quoted in the sources consulted; the title used by the anthology, 'Letter to My Nephew', is the periodical title, and the record gives both.

title: Good Country People
description: A story published in Harper's Bazaar in June 1955 and collected in A Good Man Is Hard to Find and Other Stories the same year: a one-legged philosophy doctor who calls herself Hulga is seduced and robbed of her wooden leg by a Bible salesman who turns out to be a collector of other people's prostheses.
plot_or_argument: Mrs. Hopewell owns a farm in rural Georgia and employs the tenants Mr. and Mrs. Freeman, whom she condescends to call 'good country people'. Her daughter Joy, thirty-two, unmarried and overweight, lost a leg in a shooting accident as a child, has a doctorate in philosophy, and has changed her name to Hulga in order to spite her mother; she is an atheist who believes in nothing and treats everyone with contempt. A young Bible salesman, Manley Pointer, arrives at the door, charms Mrs. Hopewell with his humility and his talk of missionary work, and is invited to stay for dinner; he mentions a heart condition and shows an interest in Hulga, who decides to seduce him in order to humiliate his faith. They arrange to meet, and he takes her into a hayloft, where he asks her to remove her wooden leg and then opens his Bible case to reveal whiskey, condoms and obscene playing cards. He tells her that he has been collecting such things for years, takes her leg, mocks her belief in nothing, and leaves her stranded in the loft. The story ends with Mrs. Hopewell and Mrs. Freeman watching Pointer walk away down the road and remarking on how simple and good the country people are. The story's ending is a judgement on them rather than on him: the salesman has taken the leg that stood for Hulga's self-sufficiency, and her mother and the tenant have seen nothing.
narrative_structure: A story in three movements - the household and its classifications, the arrival of the salesman and the dinner, and the date in the hayloft - with a short coda on the road; the point of view is omniscient and shifts between the women and into Hulga's consciousness for the seduction, and the reversal comes in a single gesture when the case is opened.
meter_and_prosody: Comic and exact, with an eye for the absurd detail (the name Hulga, the 'nice girl' with a doctorate, the obscene cards in a Bible case); dialogue that reproduces the idiom of the rural South and the pretensions of the educated; a plain narrative voice that never comments on the atrocity it reports.
historical_context: First published in Harper's Bazaar in June 1955 and collected in A Good Man Is Hard to Find and Other Stories (New York: Harcourt, Brace, 1955); O'Connor was living at Andalusia, her mother's farm near Milledgeville, and the story's tenant farm, its peacocks and its Bible salesmen belong to that world.
literary_significance: One of O'Connor's best-known stories and a standard anthology text; its handling of disability, gender and belief has made it one of the most discussed American short stories of the 1950s, and the figure of Hulga is central to the critical literature on O'Connor and on the Southern grotesque.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Harper's Bazaar, June 1955; collected in A Good Man Is Hard to Find and Other Stories (New York: Harcourt, Brace, 1955) and in The Complete Stories (1971). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The story is about the pride of the intellect and the pride of the respectable, and about the way both are exposed by a young man who is neither honest nor simple. O'Connor's own gloss - that Hulga 'believes in nothing but her own belief in nothing', and that the wooden leg is a figure of the wooden part of her soul - is the key to its theology: the leg is both a literal disability and the symbol of a spiritual deficiency, and it must work as both. The story's comedy is very dark, and its target is not the Bible salesman, who is a kind of devil, but the complacency of the women who think they can classify him.
summary: A comic and violent story set on a Georgia tenant farm, in which Mrs. Hopewell's educated, angry daughter Hulga goes walking with a travelling Bible salesman, is seduced into removing her artificial leg, and is left stranded in a hayloft while he makes off with it.
critical_context: Criticism reads the story as a comic anatomy of intellectual pride, as a study in the grotesque body and as one of O'Connor's most successful treatments of grace arriving through violence; feminist and disability criticism has paid particular attention to Hulga's leg, to the story's treatment of ugliness as a strategy of refusal, and to the way the narrative uses her body against her.
research_notes: The story was not read complete; the summary follows published descriptions and the passages quoted in the sources consulted, including O'Connor's own commentary on the wooden leg.

title: A Good Man Is Hard to Find
description: A story first printed in the anthology Modern Writing I (Avon, 1953) and collected in A Good Man Is Hard to Find and Other Stories (1955): a family driving to Florida is murdered by an escaped convict called the Misfit, and the grandmother's last gesture is one of recognition.
plot_or_argument: The grandmother does not want to go to Florida, where a convict called the Misfit is at large, and would rather visit relatives in east Tennessee; her son Bailey ignores her, and the family sets out the next morning with the grandmother in the back seat, dressed as a lady in case anyone should find her body, and with her cat hidden in a basket. On the way she tells the children stories, complains about their manners, remembers a plantation she once visited, and suddenly insists that the house with its secret panel is on the road they are taking; Bailey turns off onto a dirt road, the grandmother realizes that she has remembered the wrong state, and the cat leaps onto Bailey's neck and the car overturns in a ditch. Three men in a car arrive: the Misfit, in a black hat and with no shirt, and two boys. While the others are taken into the woods and shot one by one, the grandmother talks to the Misfit about Jesus and about prayer, and he explains his own theology - that if Christ raised the dead there is nothing to do but follow him, and if he did not, there is nothing to do but enjoy the time you have. The grandmother, hearing the shots, calls him 'one of my own babies' and touches him, and he shoots her; the story closes with his remark that she would have been a good woman if there had been somebody there to shoot her every minute of her life.
narrative_structure: A single linear narrative in unbroken time, moving from the house to the road to the clearing; the story is full of foreshadowing (the Misfit in the newspaper, the grandmother's dress for burial, the hidden cat) and the reversal is prepared by the grandmother's own error; the final sentences are given to the Misfit.
meter_and_prosody: Comic and exact in its rendering of the family, then suddenly bare; dialogue that reproduces the idiom of the Georgia family and, in the Misfit, a flatness that is more frightening than any rhetoric; the violence is reported at a distance and without comment, in the manner of a newspaper report.
historical_context: First published in Modern Writing I (New York: Avon, 1953), a multi-author anthology, and collected in A Good Man Is Hard to Find and Other Stories (Harcourt, Brace, 1955); it is O'Connor's most anthologised story and one of the most anthologised American stories of the century, and it belongs to the Southern Gothic tradition of Flannery O'Connor, Carson McCullers and Faulkner.
literary_significance: O'Connor's most famous story and one of the most widely anthologised American short stories; it is a standard course text on the short story, on the Southern Gothic and on the literature of grace, and its last paragraph is one of the most frequently quoted endings in American fiction.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Modern Writing I, ed. Willard Maas and Philip Rahv (New York: Avon, 1953); collected in A Good Man Is Hard to Find and Other Stories (New York: Harcourt, Brace, 1955) and in The Complete Stories (1971). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The story is about grace arriving at the moment of death, and about the difference between the grandmother's conventional religion - respectability, manners, the past - and the Misfit's terrifyingly coherent theology. Its central event is the grandmother's gesture of recognition: in calling the Misfit one of her own children she does what her whole life of petty judgement has unfitted her for, and the story gives that moment all the weight of a conversion. Around it are the story's comic and satirical subjects - the family, the grandmother's nostalgia for the plantation South, the child June Star's rudeness - which make the violence at the end both shocking and inevitable.
summary: A story in a single day, from an Atlanta breakfast table through a car journey across Georgia and a dirt road, to a car accident and a clearing in the woods where a family of six is taken away and shot by three escaped convicts while the grandmother talks to their leader about Jesus.
critical_context: Criticism reads the story as a theological comedy in which grace comes through violence, and debates whether the grandmother's final gesture is genuine redemption or a final self-deception; the Misfit's speech about Christ, the story's treatment of race and class in the Georgia the family drives through, and O'Connor's own account of the story in Mystery and Manners are all central to the literature.
research_notes: The story was not read complete; the summary follows published descriptions of the plot and the passages quoted in the sources consulted.

title: Everything That Rises Must Converge
description: A story published in New World Writing in October 1961 and collected as the title story of Everything That Rises Must Converge (1965): a young man escorts his mother on a newly integrated bus in a Southern city, and his resentment of her racism ends in her death.
plot_or_argument: Julian, a would-be writer in his early twenties, lives with his widowed mother in a Southern city and takes her to her weight-reducing class at the YMCA every Wednesday evening; because the buses have been integrated, she will not ride alone, and he escorts her with a mixture of duty and resentment. On the bus he reflects on his own liberal enlightenment and on his mother's nostalgia for the family's plantation past - 'they should rise, yes, but on their own side of the fence' - and he tries, unsuccessfully, to make friends with a well-dressed Black man in order to annoy her. A large Black woman in an identical hat to his mother's gets on with her small son, Carver; Julian's mother, delighted, gives the child a penny, and the woman strikes her with her handbag and walks off. Julian, triumphant, lectures his mother on the lesson she has received, and she walks faster and faster, then sits down on the kerb and dies of a stroke. The story ends with Julian running for help, calling her 'Mamma' and entering 'the world of guilt and sorrow'.
narrative_structure: A single continuous scene, from the house to the bus to the kerb, with the story's action carried almost entirely by dialogue and by Julian's interior commentary; the climax is a physical gesture rather than an event, and the story closes in the last sentence with a reversal of its protagonist's whole position.
meter_and_prosody: Third-person narrative confined to Julian's consciousness, with an irony that turns against him; long stretches of dialogue in the idiom of the Southern middle class; the story's symbols (the hats, the penny, the family house) are placed without comment, and the last sentence is long and rhetorically weighted.
historical_context: First published in New World Writing in October 1961 and won the O. Henry Award in 1963; collected as the title story of Everything That Rises Must Converge (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1965), published after O'Connor's death. It is one of the few stories in which O'Connor addresses the civil rights movement directly, and it was written in the years of the Montgomery bus boycott and the sit-ins.
literary_significance: One of O'Connor's most taught stories and the one through which her treatment of race is usually discussed; it is a standard anthology text on the Southern Gothic, on the short story and on the literature of the civil rights era, and its relation to the Teilhard de Chardin title is a set topic in courses on O'Connor.
bibliographical_notes: First published in New World Writing, October 1961; collected in Everything That Rises Must Converge (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1965) and in The Complete Stories (1971). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The title comes from Teilhard de Chardin: everything that rises must converge, and the story tests that proposition on a Southern city at the beginning of desegregation. Its targets are double: the mother's genteel racism, which treats Black people as children to be patted, and Julian's liberal self-congratulation, which is a way of despising his mother without understanding her. The story's judgement falls on Julian, since his mother's gesture, for all its condescension, is a gesture of love, and his own response to her death is the beginning of the knowledge he has pretended to have. The identical hats are the story's central image: the two women are bound together by class and by a shared world whether they like it or not.
summary: A single bus journey and the walk that follows it, in which Julian and his mother argue about race, manners and the family's lost status, a Black woman and her small son board the bus, and the mother's condescending gesture to the child ends in violence.
critical_context: Criticism reads the story as O'Connor's most direct engagement with desegregation, and debates whether its irony is directed at the mother, at Julian, or at the liberal reader; the story's use of the doubled hats, its treatment of the Black woman (who is given no interiority) and the theological meaning of the ending have all been contested, and it is central to the discussion of race in O'Connor's work.
research_notes: The story was not read complete; the summary follows published descriptions of the plot and the passages quoted in the sources consulted.

title: Howl
description: Written in 1954-55, read at the Six Gallery in San Francisco in October 1955 and published in Howl and Other Poems (City Lights, 1956): a long poem in three parts and a footnote that names the generation destroyed by madness, denounces the god Moloch, and ends in the Rockland asylum with Carl Solomon.
plot_or_argument: Part I is a long catalogue of the people Ginsberg knew or had heard of in the postwar American underground - 'I saw the best minds of my generation destroyed by madness, starving hysterical naked' - and it follows them through the cities, the colleges, the prisons, the psychiatric wards, the jazz clubs and the beds of the late 1940s and early 1950s: those who 'dragged themselves through the negro streets at dawn looking for an angry fix', who 'poverty and obscurity and sixty-five-dollar-a-week jobs', who took drugs, were arrested, were institutionalized, were lovers, were poets. Part II turns on Moloch, the god of the mechanical civilization, in an incantatory litany that names the buildings, the factories, the universities, the Pentagon, the prisons and the human sacrifice they require. Part III addresses Carl Solomon directly - 'Carl Solomon! I'm with you in Rockland' - and answers each of Solomon's statements with a declaration of solidarity that has the structure of a liturgy. The 'Footnote to Howl' adds a final litany in which everything - 'the world is holy! the soul is holy! the skin is holy! the nose is holy!' - is declared holy, ending the poem in affirmation rather than denunciation.
narrative_structure: Three numbered parts and a footnote: Part I is a single sentence of some seventy-eight long lines with anaphora ('who...') as its organizing device; Part II is a shorter litany built on 'Moloch'; Part III is a dialogue-address to Solomon in the asylum, with the refrain 'I'm with you in Rockland'; the Footnote returns to the litany form and closes with 'Holy! Holy! Holy!' in a deliberate echo of religious chant.
meter_and_prosody: The long breath-line, measured by the length of one exhalation rather than by foot or syllable; parataxis and catalogue; anaphora and repetition taken from Hebrew liturgy and from jazz; a diction that includes slang, obscenity, technical terms and the names of real people and places; spontaneity of composition (Ginsberg typed the first draft in a single session) with heavy subsequent revision.
historical_context: Begun in the autumn of 1954 and read in public for the first time at the Six Gallery in San Francisco on 7 October 1955, a reading now regarded as the founding event of the Beat movement; published by Lawrence Ferlinghetti's City Lights Books in Howl and Other Poems (1956), which was seized and prosecuted for obscenity, and cleared by Judge Clayton Horn on 3 October 1957 in a ruling that became a landmark of American free expression. The poem was written at the height of McCarthyism and of the conformity of the Eisenhower years, and it is dedicated to Carl Solomon, whom Ginsberg had met in the Columbia Presbyterian psychiatric institute in 1949.
literary_significance: The founding poem of the Beat Generation and one of the most influential American poems of the century; the obscenity trial made it a cause and its publication a turning point in American literary censorship, it is a standard anthology and course text, and its first line is among the most recognisable in modern poetry.
bibliographical_notes: Written 1954-55; first read at the Six Gallery, San Francisco, 7 October 1955; published in Howl and Other Poems (San Francisco: City Lights Books, Pocket Poets Series no. 4, 1956); collected in Collected Poems 1947-1997 (2006). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem's central subject is the destruction of the gifted by a society that institutionalizes, criminalizes and commodifies them, and its method is testimony: the catalogue form means that the poem does not argue but names, and the accumulation of specific lives gives it its authority. Part II shifts from persons to the system that consumes them, and the figure of Moloch gathers capitalism, war, psychiatry, sexuality and the city into a single image. Part III turns the poem into an act of solidarity, and the Footnote turns it into a blessing: the movement from indictment to sanctification is the poem's argument about what poetry can do, and its treatment of sexuality and of the body as holy was scandalous in 1956 in a way that later readings have sometimes obscured.
summary: A long poem in three parts plus a footnote: a catalogue of the 'best minds' of the postwar generation and their destruction in the cities, the prisons and the asylums; a litany of the god Moloch who consumes them; an address to Carl Solomon in the Rockland asylum; and a final declaration that everything is holy.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem as prophecy, as elegy for a generation, as a gay manifesto, as a document of American psychiatry and as a formal revolution in the American line; its relation to Whitman's catalogues, to Williams's variable foot and to Hebrew liturgical poetry has been extensively discussed, and the obscenity trial is a standard case in the history of American censorship.
research_notes: The poem was read in the published text; quotations are short and confined to the lines for which it is universally known. The date of the Six Gallery reading (7 October 1955) follows the sources consulted; some accounts give only the month.

title: Illustration
description: 'Illustration' is a two-part poem from John Ashbery's first collection, Some Trees (Yale University Press, 1956), the book that won the Yale Series of Younger Poets and carried a foreword by W. H. Auden. The first part is a short narrative with a medieval-religious colouring: a novice sits on a cornice high over a modern city while angels and police, a lady, a mother and a blind man offer her gifts and plead with her to come down; the second part turns from the scene to a meditation on sacrifice, art and indifference. It is one of the poems in which the manner of the New York School is most clearly on show inside a book that still reads, for the most part, as late modernist verse.
plot_or_argument: The poem works by a double exposure. Its first half is a legend or a stained-glass panel: a holy woman on a high ledge, a crowd beneath her with its offers, her refusal, her voluntary descent. The gifts are absurdly mixed in period - angels and police in one sentence, a mother's nylons beside fruit and candy - and this mixture is what makes the scene Ashbery's rather than a medieval author's: the sacred and the commercial arrive in the same syntax and with the same courtesy. Her speech is the hinge of the poem. She will not be consoled, she asks to be remembered as having accepted what she did not want, and she asks for a monument, that is, for the very 'illustration' the poem is. The descent that follows is described in the language of hagiography - 'naked as a roc's egg' - but it ends 'out of the angels' tenderness and the minds of men', which is to say out of the reach of both religion and art. The second half then turns to us, or to the spectators, and argues that something beautiful has to be given up if we are to become a larger version of ourselves: the moths climbing in the flame want to be the flame and are not diminished by wanting it. The poem closes on the evening of her disappearance - rockets, feasting, 'so many attitudes toward that flame' - and on a correction: she was an effigy of indifference, a miracle not meant for us, as the leaves are not winter's simply because winter has come. What the two halves do together is refuse the moral that the first half seems to promise; the illustration illustrates nothing, or illustrates the cost of wanting it to.
narrative_structure: Two unequal parts. The first is a narrative in short lines with a clear sequence - the scene, the offers, the refusal, the speech, the descent - and it carries the poem's only action. The second is a meditation that begins with a maxim ('Much that is beautiful must be discarded'), proceeds by image rather than by argument, and ends with a qualification that withdraws the significance the first part seemed to have earned. The relation between the halves is that of scene and gloss, and the gloss declines to gloss.
meter_and_prosody: Short, regular, mostly unrhymed lines with a marked tendency to fall into quatrains; a diction that is courteous, archaic and administratively modern at once ('combined their prayers with those of the police'); the definite article used as though the reader already knew the story; syntax that keeps its balance while its content goes wrong; almost no metaphor that cannot be read as literal stage business.
historical_context: Written in the early 1950s, while Ashbery was working in New York as a copywriter and moving among the painters and poets who would be called the New York School, and collected in Some Trees, published on 28 March 1956 as volume 52 of the Yale Series of Younger Poets, with a foreword by Auden, who had chosen the manuscript and later said that he had not understood much of it. The book printed 817 copies and sold slowly - 456 copies in four years, the whole run in ten - and the only good review it received was Frank O'Hara's in Poetry.
literary_significance: 'Illustration' is one of the poems by which the early Ashbery is taught: it shows the New York School's taste for the legendary and the banal in one frame, and it is the poem in which the two-part structure that recurs throughout his work - scene and commentary, image and its withdrawal - first appears clearly. It is regularly anthologised with 'Some Trees' and 'The Instruction Manual' as the representative poem of his first book, and later critics have read it as an early statement of his poetics of non-interpretation.
bibliographical_notes: First collected in Some Trees (New Haven: Yale University Press, Yale Series of Younger Poets, vol. 52, 1956); reprinted in The Mooring of Starting Out: The First Five Books of Poetry (1998) and in Collected Poems 1956-1987 (Library of America, 2008). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem's subject is the relation of art to sacrifice, and it takes the religious image seriously enough to make the aesthetic one visible behind it: the novice who wants monuments and who is remembered for accepting what she refused is a figure for the artwork that asks to be read as martyrdom. The second half's argument about discarding beauty to resemble a taller impression of ourselves is an argument about what spectators do with such a figure, and the moths that wish to be the flame are the audience as much as the artist. Death is present throughout but never solemnised: the descent is graceful, the feasting continues, and the last judgement is delivered flatly, as a fact about leaves and winter.
summary: The first of the poem's two parts fixes a scene: a novice is sitting on a cornice high over the city, and angels 'combined their prayers with those of the police' to beg her to come down. A lady offers friendship and is refused; a mother offers the nylons stripped from her own legs; others bring fruit, candy and flowers, the blind man all his flowers. The novice tells them that she wants no gifts but that they should remember she died accepting them, asks for monuments, and says she wants to move figuratively 'as waves caress the thoughtless shore'; then the wind unpins her robes and she drifts naked and soft downward, out of the angels' tenderness and out of the minds of men. The second part begins 'Much that is beautiful must be discarded / so that we may resemble a taller impression of ourselves', speaks of moths climbing in the flame that wish to be the flame, and ends with rockets over the city, a night of feasting, and the judgement that the girl was 'only an effigy of indifference, a miracle not meant for us'.
critical_context: Commentary has treated the poem as a parable of the artwork and its public, as a parody of hagiography, and as an exercise in the pastoral that Ashbery inherited from the French surrealists and from Wallace Stevens; the Yale Review's essay on his pastoral art reads the novice as a version of the naive shepherd, that is, of the poet himself, in a 'pastoral greenness that he may never be able to shake off'. The comparison with Stevens, first made by O'Hara in his review of Some Trees, has been pursued by critics ever since.
research_notes: The poem was read in the text printed in Some Trees and in the collected editions. Its first magazine printing was not established from the sources consulted, so the record dates it from its first book appearance (1956), the date the anthology gives; the publication details of Some Trees follow Wikipedia's article on the collection.

title: Self-Portrait in a Convex Mirror
description: 'Self-Portrait in a Convex Mirror' is John Ashbery's longest and most celebrated poem, published in Poetry in August 1974 and used as the title poem of the collection that appeared from Viking Press on 15 May 1975. It is an extended meditation on Parmigianino's painting of about 1524, a convex mirror portrait in which the young painter's face is swollen and distorted by the curvature of the glass, and it takes that distortion as a model for the way the mind, and the poem, can hold nothing without changing it. The collection won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry, the National Book Award and the National Book Critics Circle Award, the only book to have taken all three.
plot_or_argument: The poem is a single movement of roughly five hundred and fifty lines in unrhymed verse paragraphs, and its argument is carried by description, anecdote and digression rather than by theses. It begins in the painting's presence and stays there while ranging over everything the painting suggests. Parmigianino, Ashbery reports from Vasari, was a young man of great accomplishment and strange manners who was said to have become absorbed in alchemy and to have died young; the portrait's convexity makes the hand that draws it the largest thing in the frame, so that the artist's instrument, not his face, is the true subject, and Ashbery reads this as an emblem of the artwork that can never include the act of making it. Against the painting's claim to permanence he sets the movement of the mind, which cannot hold an idea for more than a moment without altering it: the meditation on the soul as a room - 'a small / Circular breathing space' that has its own weather and its own furniture - is the poem's centre. The middle sections turn to the question of what a portrait is for, and to the disappointment of finding that the answer is always the surface; there are passages on the city, on the sound of a piano, on the weather of a particular afternoon, and on the difficulty of ending anything. The last part slows down and addresses the image directly, conceding that it will outlast the poem and that the poem's own attempt to hold it is another version of the mirror's promise; the final lines leave the reader in the ordinary present, with the portrait still 'there', and with the poem's own voice admitting that it has not solved the problem it set out to describe.
narrative_structure: Unrhymed verse paragraphs of varying length in a single continuous movement of about 550 lines, without numbered sections or breaks of scene; the transitions are made by echo and association rather than by argument, and a phrase from one paragraph frequently returns, altered, several pages later. The painting supplies the poem's frame and its recurring images - the hand, the glass, the room, the weather - and the poem's movement is circular rather than linear, ending near where it began.
literary_form: Poem (long meditative poem in free verse)
meter_and_prosody: Conversational, exact, unhurried long lines, many of them end-stopped, in a diction that mixes the vocabulary of art history with that of the newspaper and the lecture; a syntax of qualification and parenthesis in which each sentence corrects the one before; quotation and near-quotation of Vasari and of art-historical commonplaces; sudden shifts of register within a single sentence; an almost complete absence of metaphor of the decorative kind.
historical_context: Composed in the early 1970s while Ashbery was writing art criticism and teaching at Brooklyn College, and first published in Poetry in August 1974, the month in which Richard Nixon resigned; the painting and the poem were printed side by side in Art in America in the January-February 1975 issue. The collection followed The Double Dream of Spring (1970) and Three Poems (1972) and appeared from Viking Press on 15 May 1975; in 1976 it took the Pulitzer Prize, the National Book Award and the National Book Critics Circle Award, and it made Ashbery the most discussed American poet of his generation.
literary_significance: The title poem is the most discussed American poem of the last half-century and the work by which Ashbery's centrality is measured; the book is the only one to have won the Pulitzer, the National Book Award and the National Book Critics Circle Award, and the poem's long, discursive, self-interrupting manner set the terms for American poetry after 1975. It is a standard text in courses on postwar poetry, on ekphrasis and on postmodernism, and Harold Bloom's admiration for it - he called Ashbery the most remarkable poet of his time - made it a testing case for the canon of the late twentieth century.
bibliographical_notes: Published in Poetry, vol. 124, no. 5 (August 1974), 247-261; collected as the title poem of Self-Portrait in a Convex Mirror (New York: Viking Press, 15 May 1975); reprinted in Collected Poems 1956-1987 (Library of America, 2008). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem's subject is representation itself: the impossibility of seeing the self except through a distorting medium, and the possibility, which the poem keeps testing, that the distortion is the only honest account available. The painting stands for every artwork that offers to preserve a life, and the poem's long resistance to its charm is an argument about what art can and cannot do. Its second subject is time: the surface is permanent, the sitter is not, and the meditation on the soul as a room is an attempt to describe a self that is a process rather than an object. A third is the practice of poetry itself; the poem repeatedly turns from the painting to the business of writing about it, and treats its own hesitations as evidence.
summary: The poem opens with the painting - 'As Parmigianino did it, the right hand / Bigger than the head, thrusting toward / The viewer' - and describes the image closely: the fur, the pleated muslin, the coral ring, the room reflected in the glass behind the head, the 'soul' that 'establishes itself, permanently, in the gloss of / This polished surface'. From there it moves outward by association: to Vasari's life of the painter, to the young man's absorption in his art and his early death, to the question of whether a portrait can hold a life at all, to the poet's own situation in a New York afternoon, and to the recurring figure of the hand and the glass. Its best-known passage compares the soul to a room that is always being rearranged, 'a small / Circular breathing space' that cannot be entered from outside. The poem returns repeatedly to the painting's promise of permanence and to the knowledge that the promise is an effect of surface, and it ends by leaving the image where it found it, in the mirror.
critical_context: Criticism has read the poem as ekphrasis and as an argument against ekphrasis, as a meditation on subjectivity and time, as an oblique commentary on American political life (Stephen Paul Miller reads it against the Watergate summer in which it was published), and as the culmination of the romantic fragment. Its relation to Stevens, to Parmigianino's own text and to the tradition of the self-portrait has been extensively discussed; the poem is also a standing test case in the argument about whether difficulty is a value or an evasion.
research_notes: The poem was read in the printed text; quotations are short and confined to the passages for which it is universally known. The date 1974 is the date of first publication in Poetry, which the anthology gives; the book appeared in 1975.

title: How to Continue
description: 'How to Continue' is the closing poem of Hotel Lautréamont, John Ashbery's twenty-first book of poems, published by Farrar, Straus and Giroux in 1992; Ashbery later chose it for his selected later poems, Notes from the Air (2007), where it is the last poem from that collection. It begins as a story - 'Oh there once was a woman and she kept a shop / selling trinkets to tourists' - and turns under the reader's hands into an elegy for a world of parties, friends and lovers that has ended. It is one of the few late Ashbery poems that readers have been willing to call autobiographical.
plot_or_argument: The poem moves in three stages and does not signal the transitions. The first is a tale, told in rhymed couplets and a sing-song measure, about an island economy of trinkets and tourists that is really an account of a small, happy, improvised society - a circle of friends and lovers whose hospitality is its own justification, and whose 'marvel of poetry and irony' is the poem's own description of itself. The second stage is the loss: the ship sails, the dreamers become sleepers standing heavily on the dock, and the tone drops from the sing-song into a slower, flatter line. The third is the departure, in which a gale orders everyone away and the community discovers that it cannot be divided - 'they none of them would leave without the other' - and goes, all together, having looked back on love. Read in the context of Ashbery's later work, the ship and the gale are the AIDS epidemic and the deaths of friends, and the poem's refusal to name them is exactly what has made readers read it that way: it gives the shape of the loss without its documentation, and finds in a nursery rhyme the cadence for an obituary. The title is then a question the poem answers indirectly: one continues by telling the story in the rhythm of a story, and by letting the last line stand as a definition of what was lost.
narrative_structure: A single poem in three unmarked movements. It opens in rhymed couplets and a ballad measure, moves into long loose free verse when the ship sails, and returns to a rhymed, chant-like measure for the departure and the closing line. There is no stanza break between the stages; the change of music is the only signal, so that the reader experiences the loss as a change in the poem's body rather than as a turn in an argument.
literary_form: Poem (lyric narrative in rhymed and unrhymed lines)
meter_and_prosody: A deliberately naive, sing-song beginning - 'Oh there once was a woman' - in lines short enough to scan; rhyme used for its nursery and ballad associations rather than for wit; a middle section in long unrhymed lines with the flatness of report ('there were no more dreamers just sleepers in heavy attitudes'); repeated connectives ('And then', 'And when') that keep the poem in the grammar of storytelling; a last line that drops the rhyme and ends the poem on four monosyllables.
historical_context: Published in Hotel Lautréamont (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1992), a book whose title takes the pseudonym of Isidore-Lucien Ducasse, the Comte de Lautréamont, and which appeared as Ashbery's friends were dying in the AIDS epidemic; Ashbery chose it as the final poem from that collection in Notes from the Air: Selected Later Poems (2007), which selects from ten books published between 1988 and 2005 and won the International Griffin Poetry Prize in 2008.
literary_significance: 'How to Continue' is among the most anthologised and most discussed poems of Ashbery's later career and the one most often cited in accounts of his elegiac manner; it is read as his response to the AIDS epidemic and as the poem in which his late style - the fairy tale that turns into a memorial - is fully formed. It appears in Notes from the Air and in the selected editions of his work, and it is a standard piece in the criticism of American poetry of the 1990s.
bibliographical_notes: Collected in Hotel Lautréamont (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1992), where it is the final poem, and reprinted in Notes from the Air: Selected Later Poems (New York: Ecco, 2007). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
