thematic_analysis: The poem is an elegy that refuses the elegiac vocabulary: its subject is a community of friends and lovers destroyed by an unnamed epidemic, and its method is to describe the happiness first, in the present tense of a fairy tale, so that the loss arrives without announcement. Its second subject is survival - 'How to Continue' is the question the bereaved ask - and its answer is formal rather than consoling: the poem continues by keeping the measure of the lost world, the couplets and the party, in the same lines that report its end. The final look back at love is both the community's gesture and the poem's own.
summary: The poem's first movement has the rhyme and cadence of a ballad or a nursery tale: a woman on an island keeps a shop selling trinkets to tourists not far from a dock, and 'it was always a party there / always different but very nice', with new friends, advice and love, each growing perfectly from the other, 'a marvel of poetry and irony'. The unsafe quarter is scary and dirty but nobody minds; the parties go from house to house, there are friends and lovers galore, moonshine in winter and starshine in summer. Then the poem's music changes and its story ends: 'And then one day the ship sailed away. / There were no more dreamers just sleepers in heavy attitudes / on the dock'. A gale comes and says it is time to take all of them away, from the tops of the trees to the little houses on little paths, and 'when it became time to go / they none of them would leave without the other', for they said 'we are all one here'; the wind whispers it to the stars, the people get up to go, and 'looked back on love'.
critical_context: Critics have read the poem as an elegy for the New York art world of the 1970s and 1980s, as a parable of community and of its loss, and as a late instance of the pastoral Ashbery had practised since Some Trees; its shift of metre has been discussed as an instance of his habit of letting form carry argument. The poem's refusal to name its occasion is usually treated as its ethical centre rather than as evasion.
research_notes: The poem's first periodical printing was not established from the sources consulted; it is dated here from its first book appearance in 1992, which settles the anthology's undated selection. The text was read in the extract printed by the Poetry Foundation from Notes from the Air and in the contents listing of Hotel Lautréamont, which confirms its position as the last poem of the book.

title: Her Kind
description: 'Her Kind' is the most anthologised poem of Anne Sexton's first book, To Bedlam and Part Way Back (Houghton Mifflin, 1960), and the poem through which she is usually introduced. It is three seven-line stanzas, each ending with the same line - 'I have been her kind' - and each presenting a version of the woman who does not fit: the witch who flies over the houses at night, the housewife who furnishes the cave in the woods, and the woman burned as a heretic who is 'not ashamed to die'. It was written in the months after her first breakdown and hospitalisation, and it turns the psychiatric case history into a legend of three women.
plot_or_argument: The poem's three parts are three historical roles for the same woman, arranged as a descent from legend to hearth to stake. The witch of the first stanza is the woman out of doors and out of mind, whose crime is a freedom of movement - she flies over other people's houses, counting their lights - and whose punishment is the sentence 'not a woman, quite', the withdrawal of the category itself. The housewife of the second stanza is the same woman brought inside: her cave is furnished, her suppers are cooked for worms and elves, and her occupation is 'rearranging the misaligned', which is both housework and madness. The third stanza is the martyr, and it is the only one in which the poem gives its speaker triumph: she rides in the cart to the burning, she is a 'survivor' even as the flames bite, and the closing line - 'not ashamed to die' - replaces the judgement of the first two stanzas with a claim. The refrain that follows each stanza holds the three together and holds the poet to them: 'I have been her kind' is simultaneously a confession, a boast and an act of solidarity, and it is what turns a poem about a witch, a housewife and a heretic into a poem about the woman writing it. The stanza form enacts the argument: each stanza begins with ordinary rhymed lines and loosens toward its end, as though the poem could not maintain its own decorum.
narrative_structure: Three stanzas of seven lines each, with the seventh line of every stanza identical ('I have been her kind'). The first four lines of each stanza rhyme on an alternating pattern that the last three abandon; the sixth line of each stanza delivers a judgement on 'a woman like that', and the refrain answers it. The poem's three-part progress - flight, housekeeping, martyrdom - is a narrative of escalation.
meter_and_prosody: Plain, short, mostly monosyllabic lines; a ballad-like movement set up by the rhymes of the first four lines and deliberately broken by the last three; a syntax of simple declaratives ('I have gone out', 'I have found', 'I have ridden'); startling compound adjectives ('twelve-fingered', 'out of mind', 'knock-kneed'); the plainest possible diction for the most sensational material.
historical_context: Written in 1958-59, after Sexton's breakdown of 1956 and her hospitalisation at Westwood Lodge, and collected in To Bedlam and Part Way Back (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1960), her first book, which John Holmes helped to place and whose title announces its subject, the road to and part of the way back from the asylum. She was studying in Robert Lowell's seminar at Boston University at the time, and the poem belongs to the moment at which American poetry began to admit the psychiatric hospital as a legitimate subject; Holmes is said to have advised against the poem's frankness.
literary_significance: 'Her Kind' is the standard introduction to Sexton and one of the founding poems of American confessional poetry; its three figures have been read as a feminist counter-mythology, and its refrain has passed into the common vocabulary of writing about women and madness. It is anthologised in the Norton anthologies and in most surveys of postwar American poetry, it gave its name to a Boston women's poetry collective and press, and it is the poem most often quoted in accounts of Sexton's relation to the witch trials and to second-wave feminism.
bibliographical_notes: Collected in To Bedlam and Part Way Back (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1960); reprinted in The Complete Poems (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1981) and in Selected Poems of Anne Sexton (1988). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: 'Her Kind' is a poem about the social construction of the madwoman, and its three figures are the three available explanations of a woman who will not stay put: she is a witch, she is a shrew, she is a heretic. Sexton's move is to accept all three accusations and to reverse their valence, so that the outsider becomes the poem's heroine and the ordinary house her prison. The poem is also about confinement - the cave, the cart, the stake - and about the body, which is twelve-fingered in the first stanza, naked in the third, and burned in both. Its refrain makes the speaker a member of a lineage, and so converts a private diagnosis into a history of women.
summary: The first stanza sends the speaker out as 'a possessed witch, / haunting the black air, braver at night', who has done her 'hitch / over the plain houses, light by light': she calls herself a 'lonely thing, twelve-fingered, out of mind', and concludes that 'A woman like that is not a woman, quite'. The second stanza is domestic: the speaker has found 'the warm caves in the woods' and filled them with skillets, carvings, shelves, closets, silks and 'innumerable goods', fixed suppers 'for the worms and the elves', and is 'whining, rearranging the misaligned' - a woman who is misunderstood. The third stanza returns to persecution: the speaker has ridden in the driver's cart, waved her nude arms at the villages going by, and learned 'the last bright routes' as a survivor while the flames 'still bite my thigh' and her ribs crack where the wheels turn; a woman like that, the line says, 'is not ashamed to die'. Each stanza closes on the refrain that claims all three as the speaker's own kind.
critical_context: Critics read the poem through the Salem witch trials and through the figure of the hysteric, as an early feminist reclamation of the accusation of madness, and as a formal achievement in which a tight stanza is made to carry a breakdown. Its relation to Plath's 'Lady Lazarus' and to Lowell's 'Skunk Hour' is a standard comparison in accounts of confessional poetry, and its refrain has been central to feminist readings of Sexton since the 1970s.
research_notes: The poem's first magazine printing was not established from the sources consulted; it is dated from its first book appearance in 1960, which is the date the anthology gives. The text was read in the widely reproduced printed version; quotations are short.

title: The Starry Night
description: 'The Starry Night' is the best known poem of Anne Sexton's second collection, All My Pretty Ones (Houghton Mifflin, 1962), and one of the most direct poems she wrote about the wish to die. It takes its title and its occasion from Vincent van Gogh's painting of 1889, and it reads the painting as an image of a world boiling with a life the speaker wants to enter by dying. The collection was a finalist for the National Book Award and made her, with Robert Lowell and Sylvia Plath, one of the three names of American confessional poetry.
plot_or_argument: The poem is short, and its argument is made by description. It begins by denying the town's reality so that the tree, the one vertical in the painting, can be the poem's first figure: it slips up 'like a drowned woman into the hot sky', which yokes the painting's upward movement to a death by water. The sky then takes over: the night boils, the eleven stars are a fever, the moon in its 'orange irons' is a madhouse instrument that pushes the children out of bed, and the old serpent which swallows the stars is at once the Milky Way and the serpent of the asylum. Against this the speaker sets her own desire without argument - 'This is how I want to die' - and repeats it, so that the wish becomes the poem's refrain and its only proposition. The last stanza returns to the human detail of the painting, the town and its people, and imagines being swallowed into the night's eleven stars. The poem's closing wish, to be drunk with 'that old, old wine', is a wish for absorption and for the loss of the self that sees, which is why the poem has been read both as an ars poetica and as a suicide note. It matters that the speaker never describes the painting's colour or its composition: what she takes from it is a movement and a temperature, the upwardness of the tree and the boiling of the sky, and the poem's own language heats up to match. The three repetitions of the wish to die are separated by description, so that each returns as a discovery rather than as a refrain, and the last of them is given to the town rather than to the speaker: the stars are where the dead are, and the poem's grammar quietly concedes that it is describing a place it wants to be.
narrative_structure: Three stanzas of free verse, the second and third longer than the first, with the line 'This is how I want to die' repeated at the end of stanzas one and two and the wish restated, transformed, in the last lines. The poem's movement follows the eye: tree, sky, stars, moon, then the town, then the speaker's wish. There is no argumentative connective and no conclusion, only a final image.
meter_and_prosody: Short lines, many of them end-stopped, with an incantatory repetition of 'This is how I want to die'; similes that are domestic and violent at once ('like a drowned woman', 'orange irons', 'old serpent'); a diction of simple nouns and strong verbs; an exclamatory register ('Oh starry starry night!') that belongs to address and to prayer rather than to description.
historical_context: Van Gogh's 'The Starry Night' was painted at Saint-Rémy in June 1889; Sexton wrote the poem in the late 1950s or early 1960s for All My Pretty Ones (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1962), her second book, written after her father's death in 1959 and her mother's in 1959 and 1960, and the book in which the death of parents, the inheritance of a mother's life and the wish to die are worked together. The poem belongs to the moment at which American poets began to write directly about mental illness and hospitalisation, and it is contemporary with Plath's own poems on the same subjects.
literary_significance: 'The Starry Night' is one of the most widely reprinted poems of postwar American poetry and the poem through which Sexton's treatment of suicide is usually taught; it is a staple of anthologies and secondary-school and university courses, it is regularly paired with Plath's 'Ariel' and with the ekphrastic tradition from Auden's 'Musée des Beaux Arts' onward, and its refrain is among the most recognised in American poetry since 1960.
bibliographical_notes: Collected in All My Pretty Ones (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1962); reprinted in The Complete Poems (1981) and in Selected Poems of Anne Sexton (1988). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem's subject is the relation between a work of art and the desire it releases: van Gogh's painting is not a consolation but an invitation, and Sexton's speaker wants what the painting shows rather than what it means. Its second subject is confinement - the moon's orange irons, the asylum, the 'old serpent' - and its third is the artist's own madness, which the poem treats as the price of the vision it admires. The repetition of 'This is how I want to die' is the poem's ethical crux: it is stated as a fact about the painting's beauty, which is what makes it disturbing.
summary: The poem addresses the town in the painting and then the sky above it: the town does not exist, the speaker says, 'except where one black-haired tree slips / up like a drowned woman into the hot sky'. The town is silent; the night boils with eleven stars; the moon, in its orange irons, pushes the children out of bed; an old serpent swallows the stars. The speaker looks at the painting and says 'Oh starry starry night! This is how / I want to die', and the line is repeated at the end of the second stanza. The third stanza moves into the painting's other life - the town, the church, the people - and the poem ends with the speaker imagining herself swallowed up, 'into that night / of eleven stars', and asking to be drunk 'with that old, old wine'.
critical_context: Criticism has read the poem as ekphrasis, as a confessional document, and as an instance of the feminist recovery of the madwoman; its relation to van Gogh's letters and to the actual composition of the painting has been examined, and its repetitions have been discussed as a technique of self-persuasion. It is a standard exhibit in the argument about whether confessional poetry can be read apart from the biography of the poet.
research_notes: The first periodical printing of the poem was not established from the sources consulted; it is dated from its first book appearance in 1962, which is the date the anthology gives.

title: Sylvia's Death
description: 'Sylvia's Death' is Anne Sexton's elegy for Sylvia Plath, written on 17 February 1963, six days after Plath's suicide, and first published in Poetry in January 1964 before being collected in the sequence of Live or Die (Houghton Mifflin, 1966) that won the Pulitzer Prize. It is a long poem in couplets that addresses the dead poet directly, and it is remarkable for admitting, inside its grief, the envy and anger that the survivor feels. It is one of the central documents of the relationship between the two poets who studied together in Robert Lowell's seminar at Boston University.
plot_or_argument: 'Sylvia's Death' is an elegy that refuses the decorum of elegy. Its first movement establishes the dead woman in her house, among stones and spoons, with two small children; the domestic detail is exact and unsentimental, and it is the same detail that Sexton used for her own life. The second movement asks the unanswerable questions - where did you go, how did you do it, why did you not take me - and the third remembers the friendship itself: the meetings in Boston, the letters, the shared nights and the shared knowledge. The poem's most disturbing move is its confession of envy: Plath is called a thief for dying first, and suicide is figured as 'our boy', a lover the two women had in common, whose attentions the survivor still wants. That confession is followed by anger and then by tenderness, and the poem ends in a series of names that are also a leave-taking, each one diminishing the dead woman to something small enough to be held. The couplet form holds the whole poem in an even, deliberate tread, so that the wildest statements arrive in the most orderly syntax.
narrative_structure: A long poem in unrhymed couplets, running to about a hundred and forty lines, with no stanza divisions and no numbered sections; its movement is associative and returns repeatedly to the same phrases - 'O Sylvia, Sylvia', the question of where she went, the figure of death as a boy. Direct address throughout, with the dead woman as the poem's only audience until the last lines, when the speaker turns to her own survival.
meter_and_prosody: Short, tight couplets with a strong caesura in the middle of many lines; a spoken, colloquial diction broken by exclamations and by repetition; domestic nouns used as the furniture of elegy ('stones and spoons', 'the tiny playroom'); personification of death and of suicide; a refusal of metaphor in the places where elegy usually supplies it.
historical_context: Written in Boston on 17 February 1963, six days after Plath's death on 11 February, and first published in Poetry, vol. 103, no. 4 (January 1964), 224-226, as part of the memoir 'The Barfly Ought to Sing' commissioned by TriQuarterly for its 1966 tribute to Plath; collected in Live or Die (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 16 September 1966), which won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1967. Sexton and Plath had met in Robert Lowell's seminar at Boston University in 1959, and the poem is the earliest substantial response by a fellow poet to Plath's death, written three years before Ariel appeared in the United States.
literary_significance: 'Sylvia's Death' is the founding poem of the Sexton-Plath relationship as literary history and one of the first poems in which a woman poet mourns another without suppressing the competition between them; it is a standard text in the study of confessional poetry, of elegy and of the literary friendship, and the body of writing it started - Sexton's memoir, the Plath biographies, the arguments about the two poets' mutual influence - has made it a document as well as a poem.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Poetry, vol. 103, no. 4 (January 1964), 224-226, with Sexton's memoir 'The Barfly Ought to Sing'; collected in Live or Die (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1966); reprinted in The Complete Poems (1981). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is about grief as a compound of love, anger and envy, and it is unusual in refusing to separate them. Its second subject is the shared wish to die, which makes the friend's suicide both a betrayal and a promise. Its third is the condition of the woman poet in the early 1960s: the house of stones and spoons, the children like meteors, the domestic imprisonment that the poem treats as the setting of both women's art. The elegy's final naming turns the dead rival back into a friend without resolving the competition, which is the poem's honesty.
summary: The poem opens by addressing Plath - 'O Sylvia, Sylvia, / with a dead box of stones and spoons' - and asks where she went after writing her last poems, how she found the courage to 'crawl down alone / into the death'. It describes her house, her children ('two meteors / wandering loose in the tiny playroom'), the domestic furniture of a life that the speaker also knew, and the telephone call that never came. It remembers their meetings in Boston, their letters and conversations, their shared knowledge of the wish to die, and it accuses her - 'thief!' - of taking a death that the speaker had wanted for herself. Suicide is personified as 'our boy', the third party of the relationship, whose 'job' of killing them is 'a necessity, a window in a wall or a crib'. The poem ends by naming Plath in a series of endearments - 'my friend, / my little mother, / my funny duchess, / my blonde thing' - and by letting her go.
critical_context: Critics have read the poem as an elegy that inverts the conventions of the form, as a document of the Sexton-Plath friendship and its one-sided record, and as an early instance of the feminist critique of domestic confinement; its couplets, unusually regular for Sexton, have been discussed as a way of containing material that the poem says cannot be contained. Its relation to Plath's own late poems, and to the question of influence between the two, remains a continuing argument.
research_notes: The 1964 printing in Poetry predates the book, and the anthology's date of 1966 is the date of the collection. The poem's composition date of 17 February 1963 is given by the scholarship on the Sexton-Plath friendship; the sources disagree on whether TriQuarterly's Plath tribute appeared in 1963 or 1966, so the record cites only the Poetry printing, which is documented.

title: Little Girl, My String Bean, My Lovely Woman
description: 'Little Girl, My String Bean, My Lovely Woman' is a poem to Anne Sexton's elder daughter, Linda Gray Sexton, written as the girl approached twelve, and collected in Live or Die (Houghton Mifflin, 1966). It is one of the few poems in her work that is unambiguously celebratory: the mother looks at her daughter's changing body and finds in it 'nothing ... that lies', and the poem's subject is the continuity of women's bodies rather than the damage they do. It is also, read beside the poems of the same book, a poem about what a mother cannot protect a daughter from.
plot_or_argument: The poem is built as a series of addresses to a daughter who is present in the room, and its argument is that the body tells the truth. Sexton begins with the garden simile, which makes the girl a growing thing, and develops it into a description of the changes of puberty that is both exact and affectionate: the lengthening legs, the new hips, the 'string bean' thinness that is about to become something else. The mother's voice moves between admiration and memory, and the memory is of her own girlhood and of her mother, so that the poem becomes a genealogy of the female body in three generations. Where Sexton's other poems of the same period record the damage done by mothers to daughters, this one records the attempt to break the sequence: the mother says that the daughter's body does not lie, that she has nothing to hide from her, and that she will not repeat the silence she inherited. The poem's ending gives the daughter away to her future without regret, and the title's three names - little girl, string bean, lovely woman - are the poem's summary of what a mother sees at once.
narrative_structure: A single continuous poem in short free-verse lines, addressed throughout to the daughter; its movements are marked by changes of subject rather than by stanza breaks - the garden, the body, the grandmother, the future, the leave-taking. The repetition of the daughter's names as a refrain holds the sections together and makes the poem a lullaby as much as an address.
meter_and_prosody: Short lines with heavy enjambment, so that the sentence runs across the line break and the poem keeps its spoken quality; a diction of the kitchen and the garden ('string bean', 'garden', 'the good earth'); direct second-person address with imperatives and questions; a lullaby rhythm in the repeated names; almost no punctuation at the ends of lines.
historical_context: Written in the mid-1960s and collected in Live or Die (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 16 September 1966), the book that won the Pulitzer Prize in 1967; Linda Gray Sexton was born in 1953, so the poem's daughter of 'eleven (almost twelve)' dates it to about 1965. The poem belongs to the years of Sexton's most intense public success and of her continuing treatment, and it is one of the poems in which she writes against the grain of her own subject matter.
literary_significance: The poem is among the most anthologised of Sexton's poems of motherhood and the one most often set beside Plath's 'Morning Song' and 'Nick and the Candlestick' in accounts of the poetry of maternity; it is a standard exhibit in feminist readings of Sexton, which have used it to argue against the view of her as purely a poet of breakdown, and its title has become one of the recognisable phrases of postwar American poetry.
bibliographical_notes: Collected in Live or Die (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1966); reprinted in The Complete Poems (1981) and in Selected Poems of Anne Sexton (1988). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is about the mother-daughter relation as the transmission of a body and of a history; its central claim is that the female body, far from being the site of shame that the culture makes it, is a source of knowledge. It is also about time, since the mother sees the girl's future in her present and knows that her own body is the past of it. The poem's place in Sexton's work is defined by contrast: it belongs to the same book as 'Wanting to Die' and 'Sylvia's Death', and its happiness is therefore inseparable from the knowledge of what surrounds it.
summary: The poem begins with the daughter at eleven, 'almost twelve', and compares her to a garden ('my daughter, at eleven / (almost twelve), is like a garden'). It watches her grow - the string bean of the title, the long-legged girl - and addresses her directly about the body she is acquiring, about its changes and about the beauty of what is happening to her. The mother says that there is nothing in the daughter's body that lies, that all that is new is telling the truth; she remembers her own body and her own mother, and the poem moves between three generations of women. Its later passages celebrate the daughter's future - the lovers, the children - and the poem ends in an act of handing over, the mother naming the girl 'my lovely woman' and letting her go.
critical_context: Critics have read the poem as a counterweight to the poems of maternal damage in the same collection, as an instance of the feminist revaluation of the body, and as a poem about the possibility of breaking the mother-daughter inheritance. Its relation to Linda Gray Sexton's own memoirs, and to the ethics of writing about one's children, has been discussed since the 1990s.
research_notes: The first periodical printing was not established from the sources consulted; the poem is dated from its collection in 1966, which is the date the anthology gives. Its composition can be dated approximately from the daughter's age.

title: The Ballad of the Lonely Masturbator
description: 'The Ballad of the Lonely Masturbator' is the best known poem of Anne Sexton's Love Poems (Houghton Mifflin, 1969), a book written during and after the affair that ended her marriage. It is a ballad in seven-line stanzas whose sixth line is always 'At night, alone, I marry the bed', and it describes the end of an affair and the ritual of solitary sex that replaces it. The title's bluntness was scandalous in 1969 and is the point of the poem: it takes the most private of acts and gives it the most public of forms.
plot_or_argument: The poem is a narrative of the aftermath of an affair, and it uses the ballad's repetitions to make the aftermath a ritual. Its first stanza establishes the death of the affair and the double figure of the beloved, who is both 'she' and 'you' - the body that is remembered and the person who has gone - and the refrain converts the loss into a ceremony performed every night. The middle stanzas are explicit about the solitary sex that the title names, and they are deliberately unembarrassed: the bed is a wife, a workshop and an instrument, and the speaker's pleasure is described with the same plainness as her grief. The arrival of the rival, 'the lady of water, rising on the beach', gives the poem its turn into anger and self-mockery; the speaker becomes 'the knock-kneed broom', the left-over domestic object. The last stanzas are the most ordinary and the most desolate: the return of borrowed books and fishing tackle, the newspaper announcement of the lover's marriage, and the final image of the town's couples together while the speaker keeps her appointment with the bed. The refrain, repeated seven times, is both a joke and a vow, and by the last repetition it has become the poem's definition of a life.
narrative_structure: Seven-line stanzas in which the sixth line is always the same ('At night, alone, I marry the bed') and the seventh varies or repeats; the poem runs to seven stanzas plus a closing repetition, so that the refrain accumulates rather than merely recurs. The narrative is chronological - the end, the grief, the solitary ritual, the rival, the ordinary aftermath - but the refrain holds each stanza at the same point of the night.
meter_and_prosody: Ballad measure and rhyme used flatly, without ornament; short lines with strong end-stops; a diction that mixes the erotic and the domestic ('workshop', 'flowered spread', 'fishing tack'); blunt monosyllables for the sexual passages; the refrain's four stresses as the poem's fixed pulse; an occasional shocking simile ('I beat her like a bell', 'the knock-kneed broom').
historical_context: Written in 1968-69, during and after Sexton's affair with a man she calls only 'the man' in her letters, and collected in Love Poems (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1969), the book that followed the Pulitzer Prize and that her publisher promoted as a book of love poems; the affair contributed to the end of her marriage, which was dissolved in 1973. The poem belongs to the moment at which American poetry, and second-wave feminism with it, began to write openly about female sexual experience.
literary_significance: The poem is one of the most discussed and most anthologised of Sexton's later poems and a standard text in the history of the literature of sexuality; it is regularly cited in accounts of second-wave feminism's reclamation of the female body, in studies of confessional poetry's ethics, and in the criticism that asks what it means for a woman poet to publish such material in 1969. Its title has become a byword for the frankness of Sexton's late work.
bibliographical_notes: Collected in Love Poems (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1969); reprinted in The Complete Poems (1981) and in Selected Poems of Anne Sexton (1988). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem's subject is desire after abandonment, and its method is to refuse the separation of the sexual from the domestic and the comic from the grievous. It is a poem about the ownership of the body: the speaker's pleasure is hers, taken in the bed that was shared, and the 'marriage' of the refrain is a claim of autonomy as much as a confession of loneliness. Its second subject is the replaceability of the lover - the rival, the newspaper marriage, the town's couples - and its third is the deliberate scandal of a woman writing plainly about masturbation in 1969, which is what has made the poem a document of second-wave feminism as well as of confessional poetry.
summary: The poem opens on a judgement - 'The end of the affair is always death' - and then, in the first stanza, describes the lover's absence: 'She's my workshop. Slippery eye, / out of the tribe of myself my breath / finds you gone'. The refrain follows at the end of the stanza: 'At night, alone, I marry the bed'. The following stanzas move through the body, through memory and through anger: 'Finger to finger, now she's mine', 'I beat her like a bell', 'You borrowed me on the flowered spread'. A rival appears - 'Then my black-eyed rival came. / The lady of water, rising on the beach' - and the speaker is left as 'the knock-kneed broom instead'. The poem goes on to return the lover's books and fishing tack, notes that the newspaper says he is married, and ends with the boys and girls of the town coupling while the speaker, alone, marries the bed again.
critical_context: Feminist critics have read the poem as an assertion of female sexual autonomy and as a parody of the courtly love tradition that the word 'ballad' invokes; others have read it as an instance of the confessional mode's risk, in which the poem's scandal is inseparable from its commercial reception. Its formal control - a strict refrain in a book of loose poems - has been noted as evidence against the view that Sexton's late work abandoned craft.
